summary.text: Multiplying by \((n-1)!\) converts the hypothesis into \(n!\mid 2^{n-2}(P+(n-1)!)\), where \(P=\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(2^k-1)\); exact valuations of \(P\), obtained from the order of \(2\) and lifting the exponent, rule this out for composites (separately for powers of two and numbers with an odd prime divisor). For prime \(n\), if the order of \(2\) were smaller than \(n-1\), then one factor would give \(n\mid P\), while Wilson’s theorem would force \(a(n-1)\equiv0\pmod n\), contradicting the hypothesis since \(2^{n-2}\not\equiv0\pmod n\); hence the order is \(n-1=\varphi(n)\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 P_M:=\prod_{j=1}^{M}(2^j-1),\qquad P_0:=1.
\]
Thus, for every positive integer \(m\), the sequence term in question is
\[
 a(m)=\frac{2^{m-1}P_{m-1}}{m!}.
\]
We first justify that this quotient is an integer and record the identity
\[
 a(m)m!=2^{m-1}P_{m-1}. \tag{1}
\]
After that, we translate the assumed divisibility into a form suited to prime-adic valuations.

Throughout, \(v_p(x)\) denotes the exponent of a prime \(p\) in a nonzero positive integer \(x\).

## 1. Valuations of the product \(P_M\)

We need a valuation estimate for products of the numbers \(2^j-1\). Let \(p\) be an odd prime, and let
\[
 d=\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
\]
be the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\). Since \(2\) is nonzero modulo \(p\), its order is positive, and Fermat's theorem gives
\[
 d\mid p-1,\qquad 1\le d\le p-1. \tag{2}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 p\mid 2^j-1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d\mid j. \tag{3}
\]
Put
\[
 e=v_p(2^d-1).
\]
Because \(p\mid 2^d-1\), we have \(e\ge1\).

For \(j>0\), the lifting-the-exponent formula for an odd prime gives
\[
 v_p(2^j-1)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&d\nmid j,\\
 e+v_p(j/d),&d\mid j.
 \end{cases} \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, the first assertion follows from the definition of the order. If \(j=dr\), then
\[
 2^j-1=(2^d)^r-1^r,
\]
and the odd-prime lifting-the-exponent identity applies because \(p\mid 2^d-1\) and \(p\nmid2^d\), yielding
\(v_p((2^d)^r-1)=v_p(2^d-1)+v_p(r)\).

Let \(L=\lfloor M/d\rfloor\). Summing (4) over \(1\le j\le M\), only the multiples \(d,2d,\ldots,Ld\) contribute. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_p(P_M)
 &=\sum_{j=1}^{M}v_p(2^j-1)\\
 &=\sum_{r=1}^{L}\bigl(e+v_p(r)\bigr)\\
 &=eL+v_p(L!).
\end{aligned} \tag{5}
\]
This is the exact product-valuation formula we shall use.

Since \(d\le p-1\), if
\[
 x=\left\lfloor\frac{M}{p-1}\right\rfloor,
\]
then \(x\le L\). Consequently \(x!\mid L!\), so \(v_p(x!)\le v_p(L!)\). Also \(e\ge1\), and hence (5) implies
\[
 v_p(P_M)\ge v_p(x!)+x,
 \qquad x=\left\lfloor\frac{M}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{6}
\]

We will also use the standard factorial valuation formula
\[
 (p-1)v_p(r!)=r-s_p(r), \tag{7}
\]
where \(s_p(r)\) is the sum of the base-\(p\) digits of \(r\). This is equivalent to Legendre's formula
\(v_p(r!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor r/p^i\rfloor\). If \(r>0\), then \(s_p(r)\ge1\), so (7) gives
\[
 (p-1)v_p(r!)\le r-1,

after which division by the positive integer \(p-1\) yields
\[
 v_p(r!)\le \left\lfloor\frac{r-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{8}
\]
For \(r=0\), the corresponding assertion is immediate.

## 2. Integrality of the defining expression

Fix \(m>0\). We prove
\[
 m!\mid 2^{m-1}P_{m-1}. \tag{9}
\]
It suffices to compare valuations at every prime.

For \(p=2\), every factor \(2^j-1\) is odd, so \(v_2(P_{m-1})=0\). Thus
\[
 v_2(2^{m-1}P_{m-1})=m-1.
\]
By (8), or directly by Legendre's formula, \(v_2(m!)\le m-1\).

Now let \(p\) be odd. The factor \(2^{m-1}\) has \(p\)-adic valuation zero. Applying (6) with \(M=m-1\) and
\[
 x=\left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor
\]
gives
\[
 v_p(P_{m-1})\ge v_p(x!)+x\ge x.
\]
On the other hand, (8) gives \(v_p(m!)\le x\). Hence
\[
 v_p(m!)\le v_p(2^{m-1}P_{m-1}).
\]
This holds for every prime, proving (9). Therefore the displayed formula defining \(a(m)\) is an exact integer quotient and identity (1) follows.

## 3. Reformulating the hypothesis

Let \(n>2\), and set
\[
 P:=P_{n-2}=\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}(2^j-1).
\]
Applying (1) to \(m=n-1\) gives
\[
 a(n-1)(n-1)!=2^{n-2}P. \tag{10}
\]
We claim that
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n!\mid 2^{n-2}\bigl(P+(n-1)!\bigr). \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, multiplying the expression on the left by \((n-1)!\) and using (10), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \bigl(a(n-1)+2^{n-2}\bigr)(n-1)!
 &=2^{n-2}P+2^{n-2}(n-1)!\\
 &=2^{n-2}\bigl(P+(n-1)!\bigr). \tag{12}
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(n!=n(n-1)!\), divisibility by \(n\) on the left of (11) implies divisibility by \(n!\) on the right. Conversely, if the right side of (12) is \(n!q=nq(n-1)!\), cancellation of the positive integer \((n-1)!\) shows
\(a(n-1)+2^{n-2}=nq\). Thus (11) is proved.

We now show that if \(n\) is composite, the factorial divisibility on the right of (11) is impossible.

## 4. Composite numbers that are powers of two

Suppose first that
\[
 n=2^k.
\]
Since \(n>2\), necessarily \(k\ge2\). Every factor of \(P\) is odd, so \(P\) is odd. Also \(n-1\ge3\), and hence \((n-1)!\) is even. It follows that
\[
 P+(n-1)!
\]
is odd. Therefore
\[
 v_2\left(2^{n-2}\bigl(P+(n-1)!\bigr)\right)=n-2. \tag{13}
\]
On the other hand, Legendre's formula, together with the fact that the binary digit sum of \(2^k\) is \(1\), gives
\[
 v_2(n!)=v_2((2^k)!)=2^k-1=n-1. \tag{14}
\]
If \(n!\) divided the number in (13), its \(2\)-adic valuation would have to be at least \(n-1\), contradicting (13). Thus the divisibility in (11) fails when \(n\) is a power of two.

## 5. Composite numbers with an odd prime divisor

Suppose now that \(n\) is composite and has an odd prime divisor \(p\). Write
\[
 n=pt.
\]
Because \(n>0\), we have \(t>0\). Moreover \(t\ne1\), since otherwise \(n=p\) would be prime. Hence
\[
 t\ge2. \tag{15}
\]

We first prove the crucial strict inequality
\[
 v_p((n-1)!)<v_p(P). \tag{16}
\]
Apply (6) with \(M=n-2\). Let
\[
 s=\left\lfloor\frac{t-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
Since
\[
 n-2=pt-2=(p-1)t+(t-2),
\]
we have
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor=t+s. \tag{17}
\]
Thus (6) gives
\[
 v_p(P)\ge v_p((t+s)!)+(t+s). \tag{18}
\]

We also need the elementary factorial identity
\[
 v_p((pt-1)!)=v_p((t-1)!)+(t-1). \tag{19}
\]
For completeness, this follows immediately from Legendre's formula: among the integers from \(1\) through \(pt-1\), the multiples of \(p\) are
\(p,2p,\ldots,(t-1)p\). Removing one factor \(p\) from each contributes \(t-1\), while the remaining powers of \(p\) in those multiples contribute exactly
\(v_p(1\cdot2\cdots(t-1))=v_p((t-1)!)\); all nonmultiples of \(p\) contribute nothing. Since \(n=pt\), (19) says
\[
 v_p((n-1)!)=v_p((t-1)!)+(t-1). \tag{20}
\]

Because \(s\ge0\), we have \(t-1\le t+s\), so \((t-1)!\mid(t+s)!\) and therefore
\[
 v_p((t-1)!)\le v_p((t+s)!).
\]
Also \(t-1<t+s\). Combining these observations with (18) and (20),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_p((n-1)!)
 &=v_p((t-1)!)+(t-1)\\
 &\le v_p((t+s)!)+(t-1)\\
 &<v_p((t+s)!)+(t+s)\\
 &\le v_p(P),
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves (16).

For two nonzero positive integers having different \(p\)-adic valuations, the valuation of their sum is the smaller valuation. Applying this to (16) gives
\[
 v_p\bigl(P+(n-1)!\bigr)=v_p((n-1)!). \tag{21}
\]
Indeed, after factoring out the smaller power \(p^{v_p((n-1)!)}\), the factorial quotient is not divisible by \(p\), whereas the product quotient is divisible by \(p\), so their sum is not divisible by \(p\).

Because \(p\) is odd, \(v_p(2^{n-2})=0\). Hence (21) yields
\[
 v_p\left(2^{n-2}\bigl(P+(n-1)!\bigr)\right)=v_p((n-1)!). \tag{22}
\]
But \(p\mid n\), so \(v_p(n)\ge1\), and
\[
 v_p(n!)=v_p(n)+v_p((n-1)!)>v_p((n-1)!). \tag{23}
\]
Equations (22) and (23) make it impossible for \(n!\) to divide
\(2^{n-2}(P+(n-1)!)\).

Every positive integer either is a power of two or has an odd prime divisor: repeatedly remove factors of two, and if the remaining odd part is greater than one, choose a prime divisor of it. Therefore the two preceding cases cover every composite \(n>2\). In view of (11), we have proved:

> If \(n>2\) and \(n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}\), then \(n\) is prime.

## 6. The primitive-root conclusion

Assume now that \(n>2\), that
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}, \tag{24}
\]
and hence, by what we have just proved, that \(n\) is prime. Let
\[
 d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2).
\]
Since \(n\ne2\), the residue class of \(2\) is nonzero modulo \(n\). Thus \(d>0\), and Fermat's theorem gives
\[
 d\mid n-1. \tag{25}
\]
We prove that \(d=n-1\).

Suppose, to the contrary, that \(d\ne n-1\). From (25) and positivity, this forces
\[
 1\le d<n-1,
\]
so \(1\le d\le n-2\). By the definition of multiplicative order,
\[
 2^d\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
and hence
\[
 n\mid 2^d-1.
\]
The factor \(2^d-1\) occurs in
\(P=\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}(2^j-1)\), so
\[
 P\equiv0\pmod n. \tag{26}
\]

Reduce identity (10) modulo \(n\). By (26), its right side is zero, and therefore
\[
 a(n-1)(n-1)!\equiv0\pmod n. \tag{27}
\]
Wilson's theorem gives
\[
 (n-1)!\equiv-1\pmod n.
\]
Substituting this into (27) yields
\(-a(n-1)\equiv0\pmod n\), or
\[
 a(n-1)\equiv0\pmod n. \tag{28}
\]
The assumed congruence (24), together with (28), now gives
\[
 2^{n-2}\equiv0\pmod n. \tag{29}
\]
This is impossible: since \(n\) is an odd prime, \(2\not\equiv0\pmod n\), and no positive power of a nonzero residue in the field \(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\) can be zero.

The contradiction proves
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_n(2)=n-1.
\]
For a prime \(n\), Euler's totient is \(\varphi(n)=n-1\). Therefore the residue class of \(2\) has order \(\varphi(n)\), which is precisely the assertion that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

Consequently, for every integer \(n>2\),
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 n\text{ is prime and }2\text{ is a primitive root modulo }n.
\]
